title: American Colonial Government
subtitle: Soldiers first, then civilians, then a legislature. Each step was smaller than it sounds.
objectives: Describe the stages from military to civil government
Explain what the Taft Commission could do that the first one could not
Explain what the Philippine Assembly was and what limited it
Explain the idea of a government that trains its own replacement

cards.title: For three years, the answer was generals
cards.text: From August 1898 the Philippines was run by the US Army. Three military governors, one after another, with no elections at all.

cards.title: 1898 to 1907
cards.text: Tap each year. The dates and the order are both examinable.

cards.title: One could talk. One could legislate.
cards.text: The Schurman Commission of 1899 could investigate and report. The Taft Commission of 1900 could actually make law.
points: **Advisory** means you write a recommendation.
**Legislative** means you write the rule itself.
**Taft got law-making power** in September 1900.
**That is the whole difference** between the two.

question.text: What could the Taft Commission do that the Schurman Commission could not?
question.explain: Schurman was advisory. Taft held actual legislative power from September 1900.

cards.title: Permissions, not job titles
cards.text: A moderator can mute you. A player can only report you. Same server, completely different power.
points: **Always ask what a body can actually do.**
**Not what it is called.**
**Advisory bodies look important** and change nothing.
**Follow the permissions.**

cards.title: Civil government begins
cards.text: William Howard Taft became the first Civil Governor. The date was chosen deliberately: American Independence Day.
points: **The army stopped governing** the pacified areas.
**Fighting continued** in provinces that were not pacified.
**Taft called Filipinos his 'little brown brothers'.**
**He meant it kindly.** Look at what it assumes.

cards.title: Halfway
cards.text: Part 2 is the 1902 Bill and the elected Assembly. Stretch first if you need it.

cards.title: The Philippine Bill of 1902
cards.text: The US Congress passed a law setting out how the colony would be run. It also said what Filipinos would eventually be allowed.

cards.title: Three things, all conditional
cards.text: The bill offered a bill of rights, an elected assembly and two Filipino representatives in Washington.
points: **A bill of rights**, but no jury trial.
**An elected assembly**, once a census was taken.
**Two resident commissioners** who could speak, not vote.
**The Assembly waited five years** for those conditions.

question.text: What could the two Filipino resident commissioners in Washington do?
options: Speak in Congress but not vote
question.explain: They had a voice and no vote. That distinction is the point of the whole week.

cards.title: The Philippine Assembly opens
cards.text: It was the first elected Filipino legislative body. Sergio Osmena was its Speaker, at twenty-nine years old.
points: **Filipinos made law** for the first time under the Americans.
**The Philippine Commission** was the upper house.
**The Commission could block anything** the Assembly passed.
**Only about 1.4 percent** of Filipinos could vote.

cards.title: You can win rounds and still lose the fight
cards.text: The Assembly could pass whatever it liked. The American-controlled upper house could refuse it, and did.
points: **Real elections. Real debates. Real speeches.**
**A veto above all of it.**
**Both things are true at once.**
**That is what limited self-government means.**

question.text: The Philippine Assembly could pass laws without American approval.
question.explain: False. The American-controlled Philippine Commission sat above it and could block any bill.

cards.title: The phrase they used was 'benevolent assimilation'
cards.text: It meant: we are here for your own good, and we will hand it back when you are ready. Somebody else decided when ready was.
points: **Every stage was real** and every stage was granted.
**Nothing was taken.** Everything was given.
**Whoever grants a right** can also delay it.
**Notice who holds the timetable.**

terms.def: August 1898 to July 1901. Three American generals governed in turn.
The Second Philippine Commission, 1900. It held law-making power.
The head of civil government from 4 July 1901. Taft was the first.
Promised a bill of rights, an elected assembly and two resident commissioners.
A Filipino delegate in the US Congress. Could speak, could not vote.
The first elected Filipino legislature, opened 16 October 1907.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Military 1898, civil 1901, Assembly 1907.**
**Schurman advised. Taft legislated.**
**The 1902 Bill** promised rights with conditions attached.
**The Assembly was real** and it could be overruled.

quiz.text: Who governed the Philippines from August 1898 to July 1901?
quiz.explain: Three military governors in turn: Merritt, Otis, then Arthur MacArthur.
quiz.objective: Describe the stages from military to civil government

quiz.explain: American Independence Day, chosen deliberately. Taft became the first Civil Governor.
quiz.objective: Describe the stages from military to civil government

quiz.text: Who was the first Civil Governor of the Philippines?
quiz.explain: Taft, from 4 July 1901. He later became President of the United States.
quiz.objective: Describe the stages from military to civil government

quiz.text: What power did the Taft Commission hold from September 1900?
quiz.explain: That is the difference between it and the Schurman Commission, which could only report.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Taft Commission could do that the first one could not

quiz.text: The Schurman Commission could pass laws for the Philippines.
quiz.explain: False. It was advisory. It investigated and reported, and that was all.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Taft Commission could do that the first one could not

quiz.text: Which of these did the Philippine Bill of 1902 promise?
options: An elected assembly once a census was taken
The removal of all American troops
quiz.explain: It promised a bill of rights, an elected assembly with conditions, and two resident commissioners.

quiz.text: What could the resident commissioners do in the US Congress?
quiz.explain: A voice without a vote. It is the pattern of the whole period.

quiz.text: When did the Philippine Assembly open?
quiz.explain: Five years after the 1902 Bill promised it. The census had to come first.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Philippine Assembly was and what limited it

quiz.text: Who was Speaker of the first Philippine Assembly?
quiz.explain: Osmena, at twenty-nine. He later became President of the Commonwealth.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Philippine Assembly was and what limited it

quiz.text: What limited the Philippine Assembly's power?
options: The American-controlled Commission sat above it as an upper house
It was not allowed to meet
Its members were appointed, not elected
quiz.explain: It was genuinely elected and genuinely legislative, and any bill could be blocked above it.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Philippine Assembly was and what limited it

quiz.text: Most Filipino adults could vote in the 1907 Assembly election.
quiz.explain: False. Property, literacy and language requirements left roughly 1.4 percent eligible.
quiz.objective: Explain what the Philippine Assembly was and what limited it

options: That American rule was for the Filipinos' own good until they were ready
That the Philippines was already independent
That Filipinos would never govern themselves
quiz.explain: The catch is in the word 'until'. The Americans decided when ready arrived.
quiz.objective: Explain the idea of a government that trains its own replacement

teacher.summary: Week 8 follows the Term 1 scope on American colonial government. The organising idea is the difference between what a body is called and what it can actually do — advisory versus legislative, a voice versus a vote, an elected chamber under an appointed one. That distinction is what the exam tends to test and it is also a genuinely useful civic habit. The lesson does not present the stages as either a gift or a fraud; it presents each one as real and each one as bounded, and lets him hold both.
discussion: Ask what the difference is between advising and legislating, in his own words.
Ask why 4 July was chosen as the date civil government began.
Ask what a representative who can speak but not vote is actually for.
Ask who decided when Filipinos were 'ready'. That question is the whole period.
teacher.extension: Have him draw the 1907 setup as a two-box diagram: elected Assembly below, appointed Commission above, with an arrow showing where a bill can be stopped. One page.
misconceptions: 'The Philippine Assembly governed the country.' It was one chamber of two, and the other could block it.
'The Schurman and Taft Commissions were the same thing.' One advised; the other made law.
'The 1902 Bill gave Filipinos full rights.' It came with conditions, and there was no trial by jury.
'Civil government meant the fighting was over.' It began in pacified areas while war continued elsewhere.
